evening.text:
It was a busy first day at D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event, in Anaheim, California, with Marvel Studios releasing the first trailer for VisionQuest. We also got the first teaser for Ahsoka S2; the public release of the Avengers: Doomsday special footage featured last month for attendees only at San Diego Comic-Con; a special sneak peek (for attendees only) for Star Wars: Starfighter; casting news for the MCU's X-Men movie; and a trailer for an animated special, LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian, coming to Disney+ next month.

(Some spoilers below. One MAJOR spoiler for Spider-Man: Brand New Day; we'll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

VisionQuest

Marvel's streaming TV portfolio has kind of been all over the place: a handful of hits, a few misses, and a bunch of middling offerings. One of the standout hits was WandaVision, followed by an excellent sequel (of sorts), Agatha All Along. VisionQuest will complete the trilogy. Yes, Vision (Paul Bettany) died in Infinity War, but WandaVision resurrected an all-white version whose memories were restored in the finale. We finally get to learn what happened afterward.

evening.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Saturday that his country struck the Progress Rocket Space Center deep within Russia using ground-launched cruise missiles.

"In Russia’s Samara region, one of the key enterprises within Roscosmos—the Progress Center, which was involved, among other things, in electronics production–was hit," Zelenskyy said on the social media site X. "Flamingo missiles were used. A good achievement."

The largest city in the Samara Oblast, about 900 km from the Ukrainian border, Samara is home to Russia's most important manufacturer of rockets. The Progress center assembles the workhorse vehicle for Russia, the Soyuz-2 vehicle, as well as the newer Soyuz-5 rocket. The facility also builds military satellites.

evening.title: DRDO Advances Pulse Laser Technology for Potential Anti-Satellite Missions
evening.text:
India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is expanding its directed energy weapons (DEW) roadmap by exploring the development of high-energy pulse laser systems capable of targeting and disabling satellites in orbit. The initiative reflects the growing importance of counterspace technologies as space increasingly becomes a contested military domain alongside land, sea, air and cyberspace.
Unlike traditional anti-satellite (ASAT) missiles that physically intercept a target, pulse laser weapons offer the potential to neutralise satellites at the speed of light by delivering an intense burst of energy. Depending on the laser’s power, wavelength and engagement conditions, such systems could temporarily dazzle electro-optical sensors, permanently damage imaging payloads or, in the future, inflict structural damage on critical satellite components.
Pulse lasers differ from continuous-wave laser systems by releasing extremely high amounts of energy in very short bursts. This enables them to generate exceptionally high peak power, making them suitable for precision engagements against sensitive optical systems. For military applications, these lasers could disrupt reconnaissance satellites, surveillance platforms or targeting satellites that support an adversary’s military operations.
The technology is considered an attractive complement to kinetic ASAT weapons because it can offer a scalable response. Rather than destroying a satellite outright and generating orbital debris, a laser system can potentially degrade or temporarily disable specific onboard sensors, reducing the risk of creating long-lived space debris that could threaten other spacecraft.
Developing an operational anti-satellite pulse laser, however, presents formidable technological challenges. The system would require extremely high-energy laser generation, advanced beam control, adaptive optics to compensate for atmospheric distortion, ultra-precise tracking systems capable of following fast-moving satellites travelling at nearly 28,000 km/h, and sophisticated fire-control algorithms to maintain beam accuracy over hundreds of kilometres.
Ground-based laser systems must also overcome atmospheric absorption, turbulence and weather effects that can reduce beam quality. Adaptive optics, similar to those used by modern astronomical observatories, are essential to correct for atmospheric distortion and ensure that the laser energy remains tightly focused on the target.
The emergence of laser-based counterspace capabilities reflects the changing character of modern warfare. Military satellites now perform critical roles in intelligence gathering, communications, navigation, missile warning and precision targeting. Any disruption to these space-based assets can significantly degrade an adversary’s operational effectiveness without necessarily escalating to full-scale conflict.
India has already demonstrated growing expertise in directed energy technologies. DRDO has been conducting research into high-energy laser systems for air defence, including weapons designed to engage drones, missiles and other aerial threats. The knowledge gained from these programmes in beam generation, thermal management, tracking and fire-control could contribute to more advanced space-oriented laser applications in the future.
The country’s successful Mission Shakti anti-satellite missile test in 2019 established India’s kinetic ASAT capability by intercepting a satellite in low Earth orbit. The pursuit of pulse laser technology would represent a different approach, providing a potential non-kinetic counterspace option that could offer greater flexibility while avoiding the large debris fields associated with missile interceptions.
Globally, several major military powers are investing heavily in directed energy weapons for both terrestrial and space-related missions. The United States, China and Russia have all been linked to programmes involving high-energy lasers designed for satellite protection, sensor dazzling or broader counterspace operations. As space becomes increasingly central to military planning, directed energy systems are expected to play a larger role in national security strategies.

evening.title: HAL’s Amphibious Dornier 228 Programme Gains Momentum
evening.text:
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited is quietly advancing work on an amphibious version of its Dornier 228 aircraft, signalling a renewed push to give India a homegrown seaplane capability for both military and civil roles. The concept, first showcased earlier as the Amphibious Do-228, has now moved beyond drawings and into focused research on how the proven turboprop platform can be converted for water operations.
According to officials familiar with the programme, HAL has already begun technical studies on the conversion and is in active discussions with the Indian Navy over the current progress. The Navy is understood to be closely evaluating the concept, and once the programme is formally vetted, it could move into the prototype stage. This would mark a significant milestone, transforming the Amphibious Do-228 from a conceptual proposal into a flight-tested aircraft.
The Navy’s interest is driven by very practical operational needs. It is looking at procuring nearly a dozen of these amphibious aircraft for missions around India’s island territories, where runways are limited and logistics are often dictated by sea conditions. The aircraft could be used to ferry spares to warships, lift crew from the sea, and support surveillance and transport tasks in shallow or remote coastal zones. In such environments, the ability to land directly on water is not just convenient but sometimes the only viable option.
HAL has entrusted the development effort to its Transport Aircraft Division in Kanpur, which already handles the Dornier 228 programme. The division had announced plans as early as March 2021 to work on an amphibian or seaplane variant of the aircraft. The idea was to extend the utility of the platform beyond conventional runways and into rivers, coastal waters, and island lagoons, thereby broadening its relevance for defence and civilian users alike.
One of the key engineering challenges being addressed is structural reinforcement. Reports indicate that the Kanpur division plans to strengthen the fuselage midsection to handle the stresses of hard landings on water surfaces, whether at sea or on rivers. Unlike runway operations, water landings can subject the airframe to unpredictable impact forces due to waves and currents, making additional structural robustness essential for long-term safety and durability.
HAL’s management believes that the amphibious Dornier could attract combined orders of 25 to 30 aircraft from military and civilian sectors. Beyond naval use, such an aircraft could find roles in coastal transport, disaster relief, island connectivity, and even tourism in regions where conventional infrastructure is lacking. For India, which has a vast coastline and multiple island chains, a domestically built seaplane could become a valuable strategic and commercial asset.
However, the road to market will not be easy. The amphibious Dornier will face competition from the De Havilland Canada Twin Otter seaplane, a platform already well known to Indian operators and often available at a lower cost. The Twin Otter’s long track record and established support ecosystem make it a natural choice for many buyers, especially in the civil sector. For HAL, this means the Amphibious Do-228 will have to prove not only its technical merit but also its economic viability.
Still, the strategic value of an indigenous seaplane cannot be measured only in price. For the Indian Navy, having a domestically supported amphibious aircraft reduces dependence on foreign suppliers for spares, upgrades, and lifecycle support. It also allows the platform to be tailored specifically to Indian operating conditions, from tropical humidity to rough sea states in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.
If the prototype stage is cleared and flight testing begins, the Amphibious Dornier 228 could represent a rare but important addition to India’s aviation landscape. Seaplanes have historically played a crucial role in connecting remote regions and supporting naval operations, yet India has largely depended on foreign designs for this niche capability. HAL’s effort, though modest in scale, reflects a broader ambition to adapt existing indigenous platforms to meet specialised operational needs.
For now, the programme remains at a critical transition point between concept and reality. The Navy’s decision will shape its future, determining whether the Amphibious Do-228 becomes a niche experiment or a regular sight over India’s island waters. If it succeeds, it will show how an established aircraft design can be reimagined for new missions, blending practicality with strategic self-reliance in a domain where India still has much to explore.

evening.title: Ex-IAF Chief Warns Su-57 Deal Risks Sinking Domestic AMCA Stealth Jet
evening.text:
Former Indian Air Force Chief Air Chief Marshal RKS Bhadauria has warned that acquiring Russia’s Su-57 as an interim fifth-generation fighter could ultimately undermine India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme if an initial limited purchase gradually expands into a much larger fleet.
Bhadauria’s argument centres on a fundamental dilemma facing the Indian Air Force: the immediate requirement for fifth-generation combat capability versus the long-term strategic necessity of developing an indigenous stealth fighter. He has argued that an initial purchase of two Su-57 squadrons could eventually grow to four and potentially eight squadrons as operational requirements increase, creating a situation in which an interim solution begins competing directly with AMCA for funding, infrastructure and manpower.
The concern is not necessarily about the capability of the Su-57 itself. Rather, it is about procurement momentum. Once an imported fifth-generation fighter enters IAF service, additional aircraft could become attractive because of existing training, maintenance, weapons, infrastructure and pilot familiarity. What begins as a stopgap capability could therefore become a long-term fleet commitment.
Bhadauria has consequently argued that India needs to put its available resources and institutional energy behind AMCA rather than allowing an interim foreign fighter to become a substitute for the indigenous programme. His position is consistent with his earlier emphasis on AMCA as a strategic national project and the importance of maintaining control over the technologies defining India’s future combat-aircraft capability. 
At the same time, Bhadauria has not suggested that AMCA can be allowed to progress slowly. His message is effectively two-sided: do not abandon the indigenous programme for an imported fifth-generation aircraft, but also do not allow AMCA to become another open-ended development project.
That urgency is particularly relevant given India’s experience with the Tejas Mk2 programme. Delays in the development of successive indigenous fighter programmes have repeatedly pushed operational timelines to the right. Bhadauria’s warning is that AMCA cannot afford to repeat the same cycle.
The concern is particularly serious because AMCA represents a substantially more complex engineering challenge than the Tejas family. It will incorporate low-observable design, internal weapons carriage, advanced sensors, electronic warfare systems, high-end mission computing and eventually a new high-thrust propulsion system. Any delay in one major subsystem can potentially affect the entire aircraft development schedule.
Earlier assessments have similarly warned that delays comparable to those experienced by earlier Indian fighter programmes could have serious consequences for the IAF. Aerospace analysis has noted that India has already lost much of the numerical cushion it once possessed in fighter strength and that a major delay to AMCA could therefore have particularly severe consequences.
The Su-57 debate is therefore ultimately about sequencing rather than simply choosing between a Russian aircraft and an Indian aircraft. India could potentially use a limited foreign acquisition to address an immediate capability gap, but Bhadauria’s concern is that such a purchase must have clearly defined limits so that it does not gradually consume the resources intended for AMCA.
The strategic risk becomes greater if an interim purchase expands because of delays in AMCA itself. If the indigenous aircraft slips repeatedly, pressure to purchase additional Su-57s could increase. That could create a feedback loop in which the imported fleet grows because AMCA is late, while AMCA becomes even harder to fund because the imported fleet has grown.
For Bhadauria, the solution is therefore urgency. AMCA needs firm milestones, rapid decision-making, adequate funding and close oversight from the government, IAF, DRDO, ADA and industry. The programme must avoid the prolonged development cycles that have affected earlier Indian combat-aircraft projects.
India’s challenge is consequently not merely to build a fifth-generation fighter, but to build it on time. A successful AMCA programme would provide the IAF with an indigenous stealth platform while creating a domestic ecosystem for advanced aerodynamics, sensors, electronic warfare, materials and propulsion.
evening.summary: Former Indian Air Force Chief Air Chief Marshal RKS Bhadauria has warned that acquiring Russia’s Su-57 as an interim fifth-generation fighter could ultimately undermine India’s Advanced Medium Combat

evening.title: Analysts Hail Reliance–Rolls-Royce Strategic Alliance as Spark for India’s Indigenous Engine Ambitions
evening.text:
The announcement of a strategic intent between Reliance Infrastructure and Rolls-Royce to jointly pursue the development of an advanced fighter aircraft engine for India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme has generated strong reactions among defence analysts and aerospace observers, with some describing it as a potentially important turning point for India’s long-standing efforts to build an indigenous combat aircraft engine capability.
The proposed partnership brings together one of the world’s leading aero-engine manufacturers and an Indian private-sector defence company, with the stated ambition of supporting the development of an engine for India’s next-generation AMCA fighter. The announcement is particularly significant because propulsion has historically remained one of the weakest areas of India’s indigenous aerospace ecosystem.
Defence analysts welcomed the announcement, with some expressing an unusually high level of optimism about India’s prospects of eventually developing and producing a domestically controlled fighter engine. One reaction summed up the sentiment: “For the first time in my 49 years on earth, I feel confidence that we will be able to indigenise aircraft engines.”
The optimism reflects the importance of having an experienced international engine manufacturer involved in the programme. Rolls-Royce brings decades of experience in designing, developing, testing and manufacturing high-performance military aero-engines, while the Indian partner could provide an industrial base for localisation, manufacturing and broader integration into India’s defence production ecosystem.
For the AMCA programme, the engine question is critical. The aircraft is expected to evolve into a twin-engine stealth fighter with substantially greater performance and technological complexity than the existing Tejas family. While India’s indigenous aerospace industry has accumulated considerable experience in aircraft design, avionics, radar systems and weapons integration, developing a modern high-thrust fighter engine remains considerably more challenging.
India’s earlier Kaveri engine programme demonstrated the difficulty of developing a high-performance turbofan independently, particularly in areas such as hot-section materials, turbine technology, high-pressure compressors and advanced manufacturing. The experience nevertheless created an important technological foundation that can potentially be leveraged by future engine programmes.
The proposed Rolls-Royce partnership could therefore provide India with an opportunity to combine accumulated domestic expertise with an established global aero-engine design capability. The extent of technology transfer, intellectual-property ownership, domestic manufacturing and future export rights will ultimately determine how far such a partnership moves India toward genuine engine sovereignty.
The announcement also comes at a time when India is increasingly seeking greater private-sector participation in strategic defence technologies. A domestic industrial partner working alongside a major global engine manufacturer could potentially create a wider ecosystem involving Indian suppliers, precision manufacturing companies, materials specialists and research institutions.
However, analysts caution that an announcement of strategic intent is only the beginning. Developing a new fighter engine is a multi-year effort requiring sustained funding, rigorous testing infrastructure, specialised materials and extensive flight qualification. The real measure of the partnership will therefore be whether it progresses from an announced intent to a funded development programme and eventually a production-ready engine.
If successfully executed, the programme could have implications extending well beyond the AMCA itself. A domestically produced high-thrust engine could support future Indian combat aircraft programmes and reduce dependence on foreign propulsion suppliers.

evening.title: DRDO Launches RFP for 256-Element X-Band AESA Radar Panel Featuring Modular TR Modules
evening.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has issued a Request for Proposal (RFP) for the development of an advanced 256-element X-band Flat Panel Array, marking another important step in India’s efforts to strengthen indigenous Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar technologies. The programme seeks an industry partner capable of designing and developing a complete radar array architecture comprising modular transmit/receive (T/R) boards, liquid-cooled antenna panels, mechanical structures and associated test infrastructure.
According to the RFP, the project centres on the development of a 256-element flat panel antenna array operating in the X-band frequency range of 8.5–10.5 GHz. The array will consist of 256 radiating elements arranged in a 16×16 configuration and will utilise 256 independent transmit/receive (T/R) channels, enabling precise electronic beam steering without the need for mechanical movement.
A key feature of the proposed design is its modular architecture, based on scalable 8×8-element T/R circuit (TRC) boards. Each module will contain 64 radiating elements and associated T/R electronics, allowing multiple modules to be integrated into a larger flat-panel radar. Such a modular design simplifies manufacturing, testing, maintenance and future upgrades while allowing the technology to be adapted for radar systems of varying sizes and applications.
The RFP also calls for the development of several critical supporting subsystems, including the TR printed circuit boards (PCB), antenna array panels, liquid-cooled cold plates, mechanical enclosure, radome and dedicated test jigs. These components are essential for creating a fully integrated radar panel capable of reliable operation under demanding environmental and thermal conditions.
Thermal management forms one of the most significant aspects of the programme. The 256-element array is expected to consume approximately 2.6 kW of electrical power, with a maximum heat dissipation of around 2.2 kW at a 20 percent duty cycle. To manage this thermal load, DRDO has specified an integrated liquid-cooling system using cold plates, ensuring stable operation of the high-power T/R modules while maintaining radar performance and reliability.
Each individual 8×8 T/R module is specified to consume up to 650 watts while dissipating approximately 550 watts of heat, also requiring liquid cooling. These modules will serve as the fundamental building blocks of the complete radar array and demonstrate the scalability of the architecture for larger radar systems in the future.
Performance specifications outlined in the RFP indicate that the radar panel should achieve a 3 dB beamwidth of approximately 3.5 degrees, support electronic scanning of ±60 degrees in azimuth and ±60 degrees in elevation, and generate an output power density of approximately 0.3 microseconds pulse width at a 20 percent duty cycle. The array is also required to maintain a system noise figure of approximately 3.5 dB, enabling high sensitivity for target detection.
The interface requirements include operation from a 28±2 V DC power supply, with control and timing signals handled through LAN and LVDS interfaces. RF connectivity will be provided using SMP connectors, supporting all 256 transmit/receive channels along with calibration interfaces. Such specifications suggest compatibility with modern digital radar architectures and high-speed signal processing systems.
Although the RFP does not identify the intended platform, flat-panel AESA arrays of this class have broad applicability across multiple defence domains. X-band AESA radars are widely employed for fire-control radars, airborne surveillance, naval radar systems, missile seekers, tracking radars and multifunction sensor suites. Their electronically steered beams allow rapid target acquisition, simultaneous multi-target tracking and high-resolution imaging while offering greater reliability than mechanically scanned antennas.
The modular 8×8 architecture specified by DRDO could also facilitate the development of larger radar apertures by combining multiple panels, enabling a common technology base for a range of military applications. Such an approach reduces development costs while simplifying logistics and maintenance across different radar programmes.
The RFP reflects DRDO’s continued focus on strengthening indigenous expertise in critical radar technologies, particularly in high-performance T/R modules, thermal management, advanced packaging and scalable antenna architectures. These technologies form the backbone of modern AESA radars, which are increasingly becoming standard equipment on fighter aircraft, warships, ground-based air defence systems and advanced surveillance platforms.
evening.summary: The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has issued a Request for Proposal (RFP) for the development of an advanced 256-element X-band Flat Panel Array, marking another important step

evening.title: RTI Activists gets No Details on Tejas Mk1 Production, Uttam AESA, Astra Integration or GE F404 Delays
evening.text:
A recent Right to Information (RTI) response concerning the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mk1 Tejas programme has declined to provide information on several key issues involving production capacity, weapons integration, radar development and delays affecting the aircraft’s powerplant supply.
The RTI application, whose response was shared by a Reddit user, sought information on the maximum number of flight-capable LCA Mk1 Tejas aircraft that Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) could deliver at peak production capacity. The applicant also asked about the projected timeline for integrating the indigenous Uttam Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar onto the Tejas Mk1.
However, the response did not provide the requested timelines or production figures. Instead, the authority stated that questions seeking clarification or asking “How, What, Which, Why, When” are not covered under Section 2(f) of the RTI Act, 2005. It further stated that the information sought was exempt from disclosure under Section 8(1)(a) of the Act.
The RTI application also sought projected timelines for integrating Astra Mk1 and Astra Mk2 beyond-visual-range air-to-air missiles onto the LCA Mk1 Tejas. These questions were similarly not answered, leaving the current official timeline for these integrations unclear from the response.
Another question sought clarification on the nature of the delays affecting the programme, specifically whether persistent software issues, hardware problems, or a combination of both were responsible. The authority again declined to provide an answer.
The application also sought details of penalties imposed by HAL on General Electric for delayed deliveries of GE F404-IN20 engines used by the Tejas Mk1A programme. No information regarding any financial penalties or contractual provisions was disclosed.
The response is significant because the questions cover some of the most closely watched aspects of the Tejas programme. Production rates, engine availability, radar integration and weapons qualification directly influence the pace at which additional aircraft can be inducted into the Indian Air Force.
The lack of disclosure, however, does not itself establish that software or hardware problems are responsible for current delays, nor does it confirm whether HAL has imposed financial penalties on GE. The RTI response simply provides no substantive answer to those questions.
The reference to Section 8(1)(a), which concerns information whose disclosure could prejudicially affect matters including the security, strategic interests and scientific or economic interests of the state, also means that the absence of information should not be interpreted as confirmation of any particular technical or contractual issue.

This strategic collaboration underscores the expanding footprint of private sector engineering excellence within India’s defense manufacturing ecosystem. As indigenous shipyards and domestic technology providers increasingly synchronize their capabilities, projects like the Next-Generation Offshore Patrol Vessels benefit from world-class domestic systems that eliminate foreign dependencies. evening.title: The ePlane Company Unveils India’s First Full-Scale e200X-PT01 Electric Aircraft Prototype
evening.text:
The pursuit of technological sovereignty in modern aerospace is increasingly forged in advanced carbon fiber and unyielding engineering discipline. Marking a monumental leap for domestic deep-tech manufacturing, Chennai-headquartered and IIT Madras-incubated aerospace startup The ePlane Company has officially unveiled the e200X (PT-01), India’s first full-scale electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Showcased inside the company’s sprawling 60,000-square-foot production and testing facility, this 2.2-ton heavy-class airframe represents five years of meticulous research, intense component de-risking, and cumulative aviation milestones designed to redefine urban air mobility.
The physical unveiling of the PT-01 prototype transitions the firm from years of successful subscale flight trials directly into rigorous, full-scale vehicle validation. Engineered with an ultra-compact footprint measuring just 8 by 11 meters, the e200X boasts the smallest dimensional envelope of any winged passenger eVTOL globally. This space-efficient geometry is intentionally crafted to integrate seamlessly with existing urban infrastructure, allowing the aircraft to operate directly from standard city helipads and hospital rooftops without demanding costly, purpose-built vertiport overhauls. Built entirely from a high-performance carbon-fiber composite fuselage, the 2,200 kg aircraft optimizes structural mass thresholds to service three distinct verticals: high-frequency passenger air taxis, urgent medical air ambulance transfers, and localized urban cargo logistics.
Underpinning its physical architecture is an 800-volt high-voltage distributed electric propulsion system driven by a patented “Synergistic Lift” wing design. By segregating dedicated motor arrays for vertical hover and forward cruise flight—rather than relying on mechanically fragile tilt-rotor systems—the aircraft eliminates critical single points of mechanical failure while maintaining aerodynamic stability at low airspeeds. Furthermore, the onboard electronic suite is powered by the advanced NVIDIA IGX Thor platform, fusing real-time multi-modal sensor streams to provide unmatched situational awareness. With type certification processes underway with the Directorate General of Civil Aviation and active ground testing currently advancing inside the GTV hangar, this homegrown airframe signifies a historic milestone in India’s journey toward true aviation self-reliance.

evening.title: Gallantry Citation: Squadron Leader Sudhir Kumar Awarded Shaurya Chakra for recovering Su-30MKI after FBW failure
evening.text:
On 09 September 2025, Squadron Leader Sudhir Kumar demonstrated exceptional bravery and airmanship while flying a low-level night navigation sortie from the rear cockpit of a Su-30 MKI aircraft, guiding an Under Training (U/T) pilot seated in the front cockpit. During the recovery phase at an altitude of 2.2 km and a speed of 740 kmph, the aircraft suffered a catastrophic Fly By Wire (FBW) system failure. This triggered violent longitudinal oscillations, drastic pitch variations ranging from $+45$ degrees to $-15$ degrees, extreme g-loads spanning from $-1.5$ g to $+12$ g, and an Angle of Attack (AOA) exceeding 24 units.
Acting as the supervisor, Squadron Leader Kumar displayed extraordinary situational awareness under physical forces that far exceeded normative human tolerance limits. Confronted with rapidly shifting g-loads and pitch under total darkness without external visual reference, he maintained complete composure. Swiftly taking command of the situation, he instructed the front pilot to reset the failed FBW channels, exercising exemplary judgment by confirming that the critical FBW red warning light was not illuminated before directing the correct switch operations.
Facing severe physical agony, blurring vision, and the immense challenge of staying conscious and oriented, he demonstrated praiseworthy intuition by promptly re-opening power on the aircraft. This decisive action averted a catastrophic accident driven by rapid airspeed loss. Throughout the intense emergency, he maintained absolute professionalism, offering continuous reassurance and leadership to the U.N. pilot in the front cockpit. For his exceptional courage, composure, and precise execution of corrective measures under extreme pressure, Squadron Leader Sudhir Kumar is awarded the SHAURYA CHAKRA.

This is a top-heavy list, led by SunZia Wind South and SunZia Wind North in New Mexico, which went online this spring and are the largest wind farms in the country, with a combined generating capacity of 3,650 megawatts. evening.title: ETMarkets Management Talk| MAN Industries eyes bigger Saudi footprint; region could contribute 35–40% of revenue in 3 years: Nikhil Mansukhani
evening.text: India’s pipeline and infrastructure opportunity is opening up a new growth chapter for MAN Industries, with the company increasingly looking beyond its traditional manufacturing base to build a more diversified and globally integrated pipeline solutions platform.After a strong Q1FY27, the company is banking on its Saudi Arabia expansion, the upcoming Dammam coating and double-jointing facility, and the Jammu stainless-steel seamless pipe plant to drive the next phase of growth.In this edition of ETMarkets Management Talk, Nikhil Mansukhani, Managing Director, MAN Industries, discusses the company’s Saudi strategy and why the region could become a significantly larger contributor to its business.With Saudi Arabia expected to contribute around ₹1,200–1,500 crore to FY27 revenue, Mansukhani says the region could account for 35–40% of consolidated revenue over the next three years as NPC, the Dammam facility and the broader GCC, MENA and Africa footprint scale up. Edited Excerpts -Q) This was a very strong quarter, with consolidated EBITDA rising 92.6% YoY and margins expanding to 14.6%. How sustainable are these margins, and what should investors expect for the next 2-3 quarters?A) Q1FY27 was a strong quarter, with consolidated EBITDA reaching ₹155 crore and EBITDA margins expanding to 14.6%. This performance was supported by a strategically optimised product and geographic mix, along with the operating momentum created by the strong execution environment.That said, we would look at margins over a full-year period rather than extrapolating any single quarter. Our FY27 EBITDA margin guidance remains at 13-15%, which reflects our confidence in sustaining a healthy profitability profile while also accounting for the normal variations in project mix and execution across quarters.Over the next two to three quarters, the focus will be on executing the existing order book efficiently, ramping up the Saudi operations from Q2FY27 and continuing to strengthen the contribution from higher-value products and markets.We would expect margins to broadly track within our 13-15% guided range through the remaining quarters of the year, though individual quarters may see some variation depending on project mix, the timing of large deliveries, and the pace of the Saudi ramp-up.Q1's print came in toward the upper end of that range, aided by a particularly favourable mix; as NPC's contribution normalises to a full quarter from Q2FY27, and before Jammu and Dammam come on stream, we would encourage investors to view the full-year range as the more meaningful benchmark than any single quarter's number.Q) You have retained the FY27 revenue guidance of around ₹5,000 crore and EBITDA margin guidance of 13-15%. Given the strong Q1 performance, is there scope for an upward revision to either guidance?A) We have made a strong start to FY27 and remain on track to achieve our revenue guidance of approximately ₹5,000 crore, with EBITDA margins in the range of 13-15%. The current guidance already reflects our expectations from the existing order book, the ramp-up in Saudi Arabia and the broader execution pipeline during the year.At this stage, we believe it is prudent to maintain the guidance and focus on execution. We have a consolidated order book of around ₹3,600 crore and a substantial bid pipeline, which gives us strong visibility. As the year progresses and we gain greater clarity on execution, order inflows and the contribution from our Saudi platform, we will evaluate the outlook accordingly.Based on the visibility we have today, we are confident our ₹5,000 crore revenue guidance holds, and we will revisit it only if execution meaningfully outperforms these assumptions as the year progressesQ) What were the biggest drivers of the sharp improvement in profitability in Q1—product mix, geographic mix, operating leverage or pricing?A) The improvement in Q1 profitability was driven primarily by a combination of product mix and geographic mix. We have been consciously optimising our portfolio towards higher-value applications while also deepening our presence across international markets.The strong revenue growth also contributed to better operating leverage, supporting the significant improvement in EBITDA. Rather than attributing the performance to any one factor, we would view the Q1 margin expansion as the outcome of a more favourable mix, disciplined execution and improved operating leverage.Q) Your consolidated order book stands at around ₹3,600 crore, with most of it executable over the next 6-12 months. How much of this order book can translate into revenue in FY27?A) Our consolidated order book stands at approximately ₹3,600 crore across India and Saudi Arabia, with the majority of it executable over the next 6-12 months. This provides us with strong revenue visibility as we move through FY27.The exact revenue conversion in a particular financial year will depend on project schedules, customer requirements and the pace of execution. However, the current order book, along with the expected contribution from Saudi Arabia and other business opportunities, gives us confidence in achieving our FY27 revenue guidance of approximately ₹5,000 crore.Q) You have indicated that Saudi operations should ramp up meaningfully from Q2FY27 following the NPC acquisition. What kind of revenue and EBITDA contribution can Saudi Arabia make in FY27?A) We have guided to for NPC approximately ₹300-400 crore of revenue per quarter from Q2FY27 onwards, Saudi Arabia could contribute to the region of ₹1,200-1,500 crore of revenue to our FY27 numbers.Q) After a brief period of consolidation, Man Industries stock hit fresh record highs on 12th August 2026. What are the key milestones that investors should watch over the next 12-18 months to justify the current valuation?A) From an operational perspective, investors should track the Company's ability to execute its strong order book and deliver on the FY27 guidance of approximately ₹5,000 crore in revenue while maintaining EBITDA margins in the 13-15% range.A second important milestone will be the ramp-up of the Saudi operations following the NPC acquisition and the progress towards commissioning the Dammam coating and double jointing facility, which is targeted for March 2027.The Jammu greenfield stainless steel seamless pipe plant, where production is expected by March 2027, will also be an important strategic development as it marks our entry into a high-value, import-substitution segment.Beyond these operational milestones, investors can also watch for progress in converting our approximately ₹24,000 crore bid pipeline into new order inflows, as well as the execution of the Merino Shelters project, which is expected to contribute ₹35-50 crore of cash flows to MAN in FY27 and ₹80-120 crores from FY28 onwards.Q) You are entering a major investment phase with the Saudi expansion and Jammu plant. Can you give us a sense of the current net debt position, the remaining capex commitment, and whether you expect to fund this growth largely through internal accruals or additional debt?A) We are currently investing in strategic capabilities that will strengthen our product portfolio and international footprint. The Jammu greenfield stainless steel seamless pipe plant is progressing as planned, with production expected by March 2027, while the Dammam coating and double jointing facility is also targeted to commence operations by March 2027.These investments are part of our broader strategy to build a more diversified and integrated platform. As of March 31, 2026, our consolidated balance sheet was in a broadly net-cash position, with cash and bank balances of ₹657 crore against total borrowings of ₹500 crore; we will share the specific consolidated net debt position as of June 30, 2026 shortly, which will also reflect NPC's consolidation from the acquisition date.On capex, our Jammu project carries a total planned outlay of approximately ₹600 crore, of which around ₹350 crore has already been spent as of Q1FY27, leaving a remaining commitment of roughly ₹250 crore to complete the project through to commercial production.For the Dammam Coating & Double Jointing Facility, total capex is approximately USD 50 million, to be funded in an even 50:50 split between debt and internal accruals.In terms of funding, our approach has been capital-efficient by design. The NPC acquisition was funded through USD 70 million of debt raised at the KSA subsidiary level, ring-fenced and serviced independently through NPC's own cash flows, with no recourse to our standalone balance sheet and USD 32 million of equity.Importantly, NPC came to us with zero debt on its own balance sheet, a net worth of USD 158.6 million, and USD 83 million of cash and liquid assets, underscoring the quality and financial strength of the platform we acquired.The Jammu project, in turn, is being funded through a combination of internal accruals and the J&K state incentive package, which includes an 18% upfront GST benefit and a 6% interest subsidy under the NCSS scheme.At this stage, we do not anticipate a need to raise external equity capital for our current growth investments, and our approach will be to maintain an appropriate, disciplined capital structure as we fund this next phase of growth.Overall, we expect gross debt including both long-term and short-term borrowings to peak at approximately ₹1,700-1,800 crore by FY27, which we see as the peak debt level for this investment phase.On capex, we expect to incur approximately ₹700-800 crore in FY27, covering the pending capex for both the Jammu project and the Dammam Coating & Double Jointing Facility.Q) You have described FY27 as an “inflection point” for Man Industries. If we look three years ahead, what will be the biggest change in the company's revenue mix, margins and international footprintA) We see FY27 as an inflection point because several strategic initiatives are coming together. We have strengthened our presence in Saudi Arabia through the NPC acquisition, are building an integrated coating and double jointing capability in Dammam and are entering the stainless-steel seamless pipe segment through our Jammu greenfield facility.Over the next three years, the biggest transformation is expected to be the evolution of MAN into a more diversified and globally integrated pipeline solutions platform. Our objective is to increase the contribution from international markets, expand our presence in higher-value applications and strengthen our portfolio beyond our existing manufacturing capabilities.These investments should help create a more balanced revenue mix and support a stronger, more resilient earnings profile over time. However, the exact revenue mix, margin trajectory and contribution from international markets will depend on the pace of ramp-up, project execution and market opportunities.Man has always been an export-led company, with exports historically representing 75-80% of our overall revenue mix, and we expect that to continue. Within that, we expect Saudi Arabia specifically to scale up meaningfully as NPC, the Dammam facility and our broader footprint across the GCC, wider MENA and Africa grow to the point where we would expect Saudi Arabia to contribute approximately 35-40% of our consolidated revenue mix over the next three years.Jammu's contribution, by contrast, will build more gradually, with its share of the mix increasing over a three-to-five-year horizon as the stainless-steel segment matures.Beyond this geographic shift, we also expect our overall product mix to skew further toward higher-value segments and geographies with better economics, supporting a more resilient margin profile over time. We will provide more specific milestones as these initiatives progress.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views, and opinions given by experts are their own. These do not represent the views of the Economic Times)

evening.title: iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation
evening.text:
arXiv:2608.06161v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

Apple faces Indian engineer’s bias lawsuit
evening.text: Apple Inc. lost an early round in a discrimination lawsuit brought in the U.S. by a female engineer from India who says her two managers -- one from her country, the other from Pakistan -- treated her as they would in their own countries: as a subservient.The woman’s case in California state court is the latest to allege workplace bias in Silicon Valley that focuses on cultural prejudices of some tech workers from South Asia. Cisco Systems Inc. is fighting a suit brought by California’s civil rights agency alleging bias against a member of India’s so-called lower castes, known as Dalits.Anita Nariani Schulze is part of the Sindhi minority -- she is Hindu, with ancestry in the Sindh region of what is now Pakistan. Her complaint alleges that her senior and direct managers, both male, consistently excluded her from meetings while inviting her male counterparts, criticized her, micromanaged her work, and deprived her of bonuses, despite positive performance evaluations and significant team contributions.Schulze claims the managers’ animus reflects sexism, racism, religious bias and discrimination on the basis of national origin. The Sindhi Hindu nationality is “known for its technical acumen” and its gender equality, she says, which “exacerbated the managers’ discriminatory treatment.”In a tentative ruling on Wednesday, Santa Clara County Superior Court Judge Sunil R. Kulkarni rejected Apple’s request to toss out the suit. While not ruling on the merits of the case, Kulkarni said Schulze had adequately supported her legal claims. Apple had argued her claims weren’t specific enough and were based on stereotypes.But the judge rejected Schulze’s request to represent a class of female Apple employees who suffered job discrimination over the last four years. He agreed with Apple that she didn’t show a pattern of discrimination that could be applied to a broader group.It wasn’t clear from the court’s docket whether the judge will hold a hearing Thursday before issuing a final ruling.Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.In the Cisco case, the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing alleged that two Indian employees at the San Jose-based company discriminated against a Dalit co-worker on the basis of caste.Cisco has denied the claims, insisting it has “zero tolerance for discrimination.” It also said the lawsuit should be tossed out because caste isn’t a protected category under U.S. civil rights law.
